Professor '''Timothy Richard Halliday''' was a British [[Herpetology|herpetologist]] and artist.

He was born on 11 September 1945 in [[Marlborough, Wiltshire]], to Edna (née Barlow) who was a housemistress at [[Marlborough College]], her husband, Jack Halliday was a biology teacher there.<ref name="Ferry">{{cite news |last1=Ferry |first1=Georgina |title=Tim Halliday obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/global/2019/may/13/tim-halliday-obituary-amphibians-global-decline |accessdate=11 June 2019 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=13 May 2019}}</ref>

He was educated at Marlborough College, then studied zoology at Oxford University, where his [[doctoral thesis]] was on the sexual behaviour of [[newt]]s.<ref name="Ferry" /><ref name="EThOS">{{cite thesis |last1=Halliday |first1=Timothy R. |title=A study of the behaviour of newts, being an investigation of the sexual behaviour of some species of the European genus Triturus |url=https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?did=1&uin=uk.bl.ethos.457899 |publisher=University of Oxford |accessdate=11 June 2019 |date=1972|type=Ph.D }}</ref>

He joined the [[Open University]] in 1977, as a lecturer in biology, and by his retirement in 2009 was a professor of biology.<ref name="Ferry" />

He played a key role in organising the 1989 'First World Congress of Herpetology' at the [[University of Kent]], and was instrumental in the creation of the [[Declining Amphibian Populations Task Force]], and served as its international director from 1994 to 2006.<ref name="Ferry" /> He also helped to establish the TRITURUS network of newt researchers.<ref name="Griffiths">{{cite journal |title=Newt Scientist |journal=FrogLog |first1=Richard A. |last1=Griffiths|date=November 2018 |volume=26 |issue=120 |url=https://www.amphibians.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/FL120high.pdf |page=7}}</ref>

Between 1990 and 1998 he seat on the council of the [[Zoological Society of London]] (ZSL), as well as chairing its conservation committee.<ref name="Ferry" /> He was also an advisor for David Attenborough's programmes ''[[Life on Earth (TV series)|Life on Earth]]'' and ''[[Life in Cold Blood]]''.<ref name="Ferry" />

As an artist, Halliday specialised in painting birds, frogs and toads.<ref name="SHCO">{{cite web |title=St Hugh's hosting Tim Halliday art exhibition |url=https://www.st-hughs.ox.ac.uk/st-hughs-hosting-tim-halliday-art-exhibition/ |publisher=St Hugh's College, Oxford |accessdate=11 June 2019 |date=5 September 2018}}</ref>

He married Carolyn Wheeler (who had been the first female pupil at Marlborough College) in 1970.<ref name="Ferry" /> They first met at nursery school. She also studied zoology at Oxford.<ref name="Ferry" /> They lived in Oxford<ref name="Allain">{{cite web |last1=Allain |first1=Steven J.R. |title=In Memoriam- The man who loved frogs |url=https://conbio.org/groups/sections/africa/act/in-memoriam-the-man-who-loved-frogs |publisher=Society for Conservation Biology |accessdate=11 June 2019}}</ref> and had three children and two grandchildren.<ref name="Ferry" /> All survive him.<ref name="Ferry" />

He died on 10 April 2019, after being diagnosed with an rare and incurable form of [[T-cell lymphoma]] in 2016.<ref name="Ferry" /><ref name="SHCO" />

The species ''[[Pseudophilautus hallidayi]]'', Halliday's shrub frog, is named in his honour.<ref name="Ferry" />

The [[Amphibian Survival Alliance]] and IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group dedicated a special issue of their journal ''FrogLog'' to Halliday in November 2018.<ref name="FrogLog">{{cite journal |title=Tim Halliday: Amphibian Ambassador |journal=FrogLog |date=November 2018 |volume=26 |issue=120 |url=https://www.amphibians.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/FL120high.pdf}}</ref> An ZSL symposium on amphibian diseases held in late April 2019 was also dedicated to Halliday.<ref name="ASA-ZSL">{{cite web |title=Zoological Society of London Symposium: Mitigating single pathogen and co-infections that threaten amphibian biodiversity |date=21 May 2019 |url=https://www.amphibians.org/news/zsl-disease-symposium/ |publisher=Amphibian Survival Alliance |accessdate=11 June 2019}}</ref>
